L1@P0: HENDRIK LENSTRA
L2@P0: I will describe a functor A 7→ W(A) from the category of commutative
L3@P0: rings to itself. The ring W(A) of ‘Witt vectors’ over A has many applications (to algebraic geometry, local rings, etc.), but I won’t discuss those.
L4@P0: Convention: rings have 1’s that are respected by ring homomorphisms. By
L5@P0: A I will always denote a commutative ring.
L6@P0: The literature on the functor W is in a somewhat unsatisfactory state:
L7@P0: nobody seems to have any interest in Witt vectors beyond applying them for
L8@P0: a purpose, and they are often treated in appendices to papers devoting to
L9@P0: something else; also, the construction usually depends on a set of implicit or
L10@P0: unintelligible formulae. Apparently, anybody who wishes to understand Witt
L11@P0: vectors needs to construct them personally. That is what is now happening
L12@P0: to myself.
L13@P0: One may compare the construction of W(A) to the construction of the
L14@P0: polynomial ring A[X]: the ring operations in the latter are also defined by
L15@P0: formulae, but those are both explicit and intelligible. In addition, A[X] can
L16@P0: be thought of in a conceptual way: it is an A-algebra that represents the
L17@P0: forgetful functor from the category of A-algebras to the category of sets. It is
L18@P0: quite possible that W(A) also represents some functor, and that this helps in
L19@P0: constructing W; but I never saw a satisfactory treatment along these lines.
L20@P0: For W(A), the arrows run in the opposite direction: A is a W(A)-algebra
L21@P0: rather than the other way around, and if W(A) represents a functor then
L22@P0: most likely it is a contravariant one.
L23@P0: If the only available way to construct W is by implicit formulae, then
L24@P0: one is doomed to using those formulae whenever one wishes to prove any
L25@P0: result about Witt vectors. The theory as found in the literature is indeed
L26@P0: formula-ridden.
L27@P0: My treatment depends also on a formula (see (ii) below), but it is both
L28@P0: explicit and intelligible. One may be hopeful that my approach will pass

L362: ### 2.5 Constructing $c$-related polygons
L363: 
L364: In this section we describe a construction that yields a pair of $c$-related $n$-gons. This is a centroaffine analog of a construction that yields pairs of polygons in the discrete bicycle correspondence that is described in [cite31†13 ].
L365: Assume first that $n$ is odd. Start with an $n$-gon (pentagon ${\mathbf{A}}$ in Figure cite65†6 ). Connect the midpoints of its sides with the origin. Consider the affine reflections in these lines that interchange the vertices of the respective sides of ${\mathbf{A}}$. Let $R$ be the composition of these reflections taken around the polygon.
L366: 
L367: Figure 6: Constructing a $c$-related pair of $n$-gons, odd $n$.
L368: ###### Lemma 2.8.
L369: 
L370: The map $R$ is an affine reflection.
L371: ###### Proof.
L372: 
L373: Since $n$ is odd, $R$ is orientation reversing and its determinant equals $-1$. Hence it has two eigendirections. Also $R$ has a fixed point, a vertex of ${\mathbf{A}}$. Therefore the eigenvalues of $R$ are $1$ and $-1$, and it is an affine reflection. ∎
L374: 
L375: It follows that $R^{2}=Id$. The construction of a $c$-related pair follows.
L376: 
L377: Start with an arbitrary point $P_{1}$ and apply consecutive affine reflections around the polygon ${\mathbf{A}}$ twice. This produces $2n$ points
L378:  | $$P_{1}\mapsto Q_{2}\mapsto P_{3}\mapsto Q_{4}\mapsto\cdots\mapsto Q_{n},$$  |
L379: 
L380: see cite65†6 . Each quadrilateral $P_{i}P_{i+1}Q_{i}Q_{i+1}$ is a centroaffine butterfly, therefore ${\bf P}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\sim}}{\bf Q}$.
L381: 
L382: One has $c=[P_{1},Q_{1}]=[P_{1},R(P_{1})]$. The locus of points $P_{1}$ for which $[P_{1},R(P_{1})]$ is fixed is a hyperbola (indeed, $R$ is conjugated to the map $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y)$, in which case this claim is obvious).
L383: Now consider the case of even $n$. We repeat the above construction, but this time the transformation $R$ had determinant 1. It still has an eigendirection with eigenvalue 1 (a vertex of ${\bf A}$ is a fixed point), but it is not necessarily the identity. We need to assume that $R=Id$, see below.
